p:
So the City Council has released an estimated number of $92

million for 86 companies. That's about half of the companies. It would be $173 if you were to expand it citywide–
[interposing] And do you think those estimates were roughly accurate based on your assessment?
For order of magnitude purposes.
So roughly we're talking about $180 million to go citywide, fifth firefighter?
That would be the city council estimate.
And no independent perspective from the Fire Department? You think that that's roughly broad strokes? That seems like a reasonable estimate.
I think order of magnitude, that's about right. I mean, we're in conversation with OMB about the estimate. We have some–

And, you know, I've really appreciate it, and I don't mean to cut

you off— you, I– you're one of the best finance directors at any agency in the city, so I know you know the answers to all these questions. And I will push because there are some folks that could sit up on this panel and wouldn't be able to answer questions. You are not one of them. So, I appreciate you coming back to us. And I really appreciate, Commissioner, you coming in with a very forceful position on supporting EMS workers. Any orders of magnitude? There have been a range of approaches on pay equity. I know that it's subject to negotiations, but can you speak to the range of costs that have been discussed to improve compensation for EMS?

So this is not speaking to the range, but I know that we have deferred to OLR on what it would cost. Maybe just to put some context around what the scale is, the average EMT salary, looking at base salary and additions to gross but not including overtime, is $57,494. The average firefighter salary, base salary, additions to gross, no overtime, is $109,930. So, it's almost double. It's 91 percent higher.

And so if we were to double the salary of every EMS worker, which is— if I don't think is the likely outcome, but something along those— if— how much would that cost us? Do you have a broad sense of— I mean, I've seen estimates that have ranged– that EMS is advocating— EMTs have advocating for increases in wages from $80 million up to $200 million or even more, potentially over a multi-year. Comparable number— I mean, numbers that are in a similar ballpark to what we could be talking about for a fifth firefighter. Considering how dire the situation is with EMT worker retention, in a world of limited resources, I really do hope that we focus on fixing this crisis that we have at EMT. The fact that after five years an EMT can't make more than $59,000 is disgraceful. And I never— I– the starting salary in my office is north of that. And frankly, these are kids coming out of college who are great and bright and amazing, and I'm lucky to have them. But a person who's spent five years saving lives across the city of New York deserves more and deserves better. So I really— and then coming back, if we were to add a fifth firefighter at a cost of

approximately $180 million citywide– I'll ask Commissioner or Chief, if you were handed a bucket of $180 million in cash and were told that you could do anything in your power to reduce fire fatalities in the City of New York, is hiring a fifth firefighter at the top of your list? Do you think that would have the greatest impact?

And that's what we're looking at. We're trying to figure out what would have the greatest impact. It would have an impact. I don't know if that would be the greatest impact in every company around the city.
I'd imagine that we could look a lot—
[interposing] If I had that bucket of money—
Yeah.
Right? Certainly, EMS pay would be the top of the list.

I certainly appreciate that too. I share that priority. We're on the same page. In— for the— narrower purpose question of how do we address what we have as a crisis of

fires in the Bronx and situations that need to be resolved, fire prevention investments, investments to address the most concerning housing stock, there are a variety of different targeted ways that we could probably smartly spend a whole lot less resources that could have a bigger impact in reducing fatalities from fire than a fifth firefighter and an extraordinary cost cost of $180 million citywide. Is that fair?
I think that's fair.

So recognizing that, and also recognizing that you said that the fifth firefighter, the thing where they have the greatest impact is getting the hose out and getting water out. Firestock in the Bronx, six, seven-story buildings. Is that the height of buildings that we need to get that fifth firefighter in place? Are those the areas that you would prioritize it having the greatest impact?

As a general statement, yes. Right? It's a longer hose line stretch, 75 feet, 70-75 feet tall is the height of a building. Above

that you need a standpipe in it, which is different from stretching off the apparatus.

And then just to make sure I got this right on the record, you said that the response times in Queens and Staten Island are slower than in the Bronx? You had five minutes and 10 seconds in Queens and five minutes and two seconds— five minutes and 10 seconds in Queens, five minutes in– five minutes and five seconds in Queens, five minutes and two seconds in Staten Island. Did I have those right? The Bronx was ranked third in terms of response time citywide.
So Bronx was four minutes 58 seconds, Queens was five minutes two seconds, Staten Island five minutes five seconds.
Okay, so all about the same.
And that’s year-to-date average response time to structural fires.

Okay. I really appreciate the qu— the responses. I'm sorry to get frustrated earlier. I just think in a world where we have limited resources, we want to invest them in the

places that are going to make the greatest difference in saving lives. And we do have a crisis in the Bronx that I'm very committed to advocating for with my colleagues. I have seen the— I've seen Council Member Pierina Sanchez in particular out on site with the men and women of the FDNY, just in dire situations. We do need to do more up there. I just want to make sure we're spending our money smartly, and that's an extraordinary expense that we don't have data to back up the difference that it would make. And so I hope we can be smart about how we prioritize things from here. Thank you.
Chair Ariola?

Thank you. So, I know that you said that you don't have any real data about the fifth firefighter and whether or not it– the fifth firefighter helps. We have opinions that we've been sharing back and forth, but there have been independent studies done, and I do have one here where it notes that the fifth firefighter makes a difference by eliminating kinks and drag, which you guys know the lingo, enables the hose shuffle, frees the pump operator, puts water faster on the fire, and

reduces firefighter fatigue. Would you agree with that?
I think that's an accurate statement.

So getting more staffing in the busiest companies will put a line in a place quicker, limit the spread of a fire and the loss of life and the displacement of residents. At the same time, reduce the strain on firefighters operating on that fire. Would you agree with that?
As a general statement, yes.
Okay. I'm going to move on to– well, does the Fire Department have a platform that tracks and prioritizes work order requests, assessments, and resolution?
Yes, we do. We have an asset management–
[interposing] I'm sorry, I didn't hear you. I'm sorry.
Yes, we do. We have an EAM. It's an asset management program.
Okay. And you use the Niedermann systems as well, or—
Yes, we have Niedermann systems.
Niedermann system. And how many systems are inoperable right now?
Zero.
Zero. They're all operable?
Yes.

Oh, okay. All right. Okay. Let's see. The FDNY has publicly cited a substantial backlog of capital projects. Yet the financial plan pushes the vast majority of the facilities funding to the out years. Meanwhile, we have identified a list of firehouses with severely deteriorating roofs, of which only six projects have been funded to date. We have serious concerns about deferred maintenance, the adequacy of near-term capital funding, and the administration's reliance on councilmember allocations to fund what could be core infrastructure. Do you have an amount needed to

repair all capital projects, and have you requested that from the administration?

So, to talk about facilities funding in general, so our current capital plan includes $994 million for facilities across FY26 through FY35. The funding is split pretty evenly between the first five years and the last five years. It's actually slightly front-loaded. So FY26 through FY30 is $553 million, whereas FY31 through FY35 is $441 million. But even with that, I mean, we have many facilities. We have over 400 buildings, and they are old. So the average age of our firehouses is approaching 100 years old, and so the— our state of good repair needs have exceeded our budget. I think we are seeing the budget move in the right direction. So this plan includes an additional $24 million for roofs. And, you know, we have also seen that our capital funding for facilities over the last five years has nearly doubled. We've seen significant adds to our budget over the last five years.

Yet many firehouses remain in disrepair, a few of which— and a number of

you, Commissioner, our Chief, and certainly Paul, we were out there looking at them. So, how can you take this pool of funding that is pushed into the out years and encourage the administration to bring that funding forward?

So, we do have conversations with OMB about project accelerations, and the Executive Budget did include some funding accelerations on the facility side. It included accelerating $11.7 million into next year, for renovations at one of our fleet maintenance buildings, which will expand capacity. It included accelerations of $1.7 million into 27 and $10.1 million into 28 for multi-component renovations at EMS Station Four. It included $10.5 million into FY27 to replace the apparatus floor at Engine Company 163, and $6.8 million into FY27 to replace air compressors at our mask services unit. I think there are lots of projects that we're looking at to see if there's a potential for acceleration. Bandwidth is a part of this too. So the additional civilian headcount that was added in this plan will be incredibly beneficial towards getting more projects done. So that will

allow us to hire more trade staff and facilities to make repairs, it will help with our project management capabilities, will help with procurement. So we've lost a lot of procurement staff, and adding back some of those folks will help get those design and construction contracts that we need to get that capital work moving done faster.

Okay. So realistically, we're not going to see any of this money anytime soon, because once it goes into the far-out years, like 35, it oftentimes evaporates. As you know, because we have a lot of firehouses, you said are nearing 100 years old, and there hasn't been a nickel put into them in 100 years, and we've seen the result of that, which is complete deterioration. We have work orders in for 25 years that have not been fulfilled, and we'll get into that later on. We've identified a list of firehouses with severely deteriorating roofs, totaling approximately $80.9 million in estimated need as of 2024 with costs now escalating further. So that's the other problem. As we push further into the out-years, the cost of fixing that firehouse, that issue, that EMS station

is much larger. So we don't have the money to cover it fully. And a lot of it gets eaten up in the design process. And that's what we're trying to stop. So six of those projects have since been funded, right? Engine 62, 96, 156, 264, 304, and 329, that's right? Okay. What is the status of the remaining underfunded roof projects by the list that my office gave to the Fire Department, and when does the Department expect to address them?

So first, we just want to express our appreciation, because one of those roofs was funded by you, Council Member Ariola. Actually, several of those roofs were funded by council members. So there was funding provided by Council Member Riley, Farias, and Carr. And you were also instrumental in getting some of that roof funding added for the Big House, which was another one of the roofs on the list. So for the remaining roofs, that's what the funding that was added for the six roofs will go towards. It will help us prioritize the next six roofs that are unfunded. We do have some roof projects already underway, which I will defer to Commissioner DeRocchis to talk about.

Thank you. Hi. We definitely do have some roofs that are on the way. Some are already completed or nearing completion. That would be Engine 325, Engine 161, Engine Company 54, Engine 74, and Engine 301. And we are constantly assessing the conditions of our roofs with our trade staff, and we do as much of the repairs as we possibly can while we are constantly working with the OMB to accelerate that funding forwards if possible.

Okay. And as you mentioned, a lot of those roofs that are already funded came from council members that were funding in their own districts. And the Big House, Council Member Selvena Brooks-Powers advocated for that. I advocated for that. And we saw the disrepair there, but the funding is fully there. But why is it always on the City Council? Why doesn't the administration take care of their buildings? When we visited buildings throughout the five boroughs, the condition of those buildings, if visited by the Fire Department, or the DOB, no one would be able to inhabitate them. And that's a problem. So many of the

buildings on this list that I— that we provided for you, which I'm looking to see here. Okay, none of which made your list, but okay. You know, were constructed between 1895 and 1929. That– you know, the Fire Department has to advocate for these projects, not just rely on the City Council. So how many of these projects were sent by the Fire Department to the admin asking for funding to complete them? Was it just the six?

So we have had conversations with OMB and City Hall on all of our capital needs. And so they are certainly aware of the condition of our facilities, and the broad needs that we've identified for them. But we do operate under funding constraints, and so the six are sort of the priority ones that have been identified and funded.
Right, but they won't be even addressed until 2035, is that correct?
The funding is currently in fiscal 31, and we're currently assessing to see if it's possible to accelerate.
All right. And of the list that the office provided you, how many of those projects did you send to council members, when you were asking for budget priority requests?
We can double-check, but probably quite a few of them.
Anybody here get a request? Okay, none of us. Okay. I see that Council Member Hudson has come back into the room, and I'm going to defer to her right now for her to ask her questions.

Thank you so much, Chairs, and I appreciate it. I had to run to another meeting, so my apologies. And please do tell me if these questions have been asked, but I do want to just jump in on the capital piece. I don't know all of the questions that Chair Ariola has already asked, but just want to say that in your testimony you referenced some capital dollars in this fiscal year as well as the out-years, and by my count, the funding would go towards the renovations of about eight buildings or so, and I was just curious to know what percentage, that represents of your entire

physical infrastructure that needs repair? Stations, firehouses, any other properties?
So I think the things that were mentioned in the testimony were probably the roofs that were just funded.
Yeah, six roofs.
Six, and then there were a few projects that were accelerated, but those are not the only projects funded. There are many more projects actually funded. Those were just the ones that—
[interposing] Many more that are funded?
Yes, many more.
Capital— many more capital improvements that are funded already?
Yes. So, of your total capital needs, how many of the projects would you say are funded? Like 50 percent, 80 percent, 10 percent?
I mean, our capital needs are significant.
Are great, I know, that's what I'm getting at. I'm trying to help you.
But we do have, you know, as I said, $994 million across the 10-year plan for capital and $553 million of that is in the first five years of the plan.
So almost half?
Yes.
Roughly.
About half.
So if that $994 was a number?
Yes.
$994 million is completed, then all your capital needs are taken care of?
No. I mean, there are— as I said before, given the number of our facilities and their current state of repair, our capital needs, you know, are— go beyond our existing funding.

Okay. So I'm just trying to figure out what of the existing funding that's been allocated to address capital needs, what percentage of that— what percentage is that of the total capital needs you have?
I would have to say it's about 25 to 30 percent.

25 to 30 percent, okay. So, I'm not going to attempt to do quick math in my head. But $100 million, roughly speaking, or $994 million, you said, is about 25 to 30 percent of your total needs. Or is it the $500 million?
I believe it's the $500 million.
The $500 million is 25 to 30 percent of your total capital needs? Okay.
I don't think we have it quantified that way. I think, you know, we have 400 or so buildings. Many of these buildings are a century year-old.
Yep.

Those capital projects will continue to pop up as we go forward. I don't think there's any place where we could say all our capital needs will be secured and done if you give us this amount of money, because it's a rotating thing. It's, you know, as the buildings age, more and more things things pop up.
Yeah.

So that's— I think that's what you see in, like, why we're struggling to try to give you an actual percentage. The money that we have is the money that's going to go towards the capital– the most needed capital projects.
Good. Okay.

Yeah, I was just gonna add for, for context, I mentioned this earlier, but I don't know if it was when you were out. So we have seen our capital funding for facilities increased pretty substantially in the last five years. If you looked five years ago, so in 2021, our facilities funding was only about 37 percent of our capital budget, and now it's more than half. It's

52 percent of our capital budget. It's grown by nearly $500 million. So–
[interposing] Okay, that's great.
There's still a lot of state of good repair needs–
[interposing] Yeah.

that we have to address, but we are seeing the budget move in the right direction towards funding those state of good repair needs. And another component of this is really having the bandwidth in terms of civilian staff to actually execute those projects. And so the–
[interposing] Okay.

the 84 civilian positions that we got in this budget are instrumental towards doing that. Both staff for facilities and for procurement to execute on those design and construction contracts that we need.

Okay. Thank you. I appreciate it. And I'm– you know, not trying to be

difficult, just I'm trying to get down to the fact that I would argue you could use far more capital dollars to address the needs at all of your buildings. And so I think you could probably agree with that sentiment, perhaps.
More money would solve more problems.

There you go. Okay. Great. And then I just want— did anyone ask about cold weather events yet? Okay. If I can just ask a couple questions. What percentage increase in EMS calls occurs during extreme cold weather events compared to normal conditions?

I don't know if we have the exact number. Do you have the exact number? I don't think we have the exact number of what percentage, but certainly this last winter that was way colder than any other winter we remember, and for a longer period of time, we saw a significant number increase in call volume. And as part of the city's engagement with the folks that were out in the field, we were right front center stage on that. So, anytime that we see stretches of bad weather, whether

it be cold or hot, the call volume goes up for us. I– and it goes, it goes up both on fire and
Right. Maybe you can follow up with the specifics.
Yeah, we can get back to you with that.
Okay, thank you. And then, what additional budget allocations have been designated for extreme cold weather operations?
We haven't had any specific budget adjustments tied to extreme cold weather. I mean–
[interposing] Okay.
to the extent that, you know, we've incurred additional overtime costs, that's been part of the adjustments that were made in the last budget for our PS budget.

I mean, I would suggest that just given where we're going globally in terms of climate change and all of that, and like you mentioned, Commissioner, the winters are going to get colder and longer, the summer's going to get hotter

and longer. You know, I would strongly advocate for more funding or adjusted funding to accommodate, you know, overtime and the needs as they grow during those extreme weather conditions. And then just one last question, Chairs. What's the demographic breakdown of applicants versus hires as far as percentages by race and gender.
Let Commissioner Noonan talk to you about that.
Are you referring to our firefighter applicants?
Both, if you have it.
I would have it for the fire applicants.
Okay, I'll take what you have.

Okay. So our most recent exam, we hired— we had about 20,000— over 20,607 passers. 22 percent of those passers were Black, 28 percent Hispanic, 40 percent white, and six percent Asian, seven percent were women.
Are passers hired?

They're not hired. We haven't actually hired any of these candidates yet. They're just now going through the first step, which is passing the physical exam. So that will continue through the end of June, and then they'll start the background process.
Do you have any of those statistics for previous fiscal years?
I probably do. So for our previous firefighter exam– give me a moment. Where did I put it? If you give me a second, I'll—
[interposing] Sure.

where I put it. So for the last— the last exam, we had– in terms of our test takers, we had 28 percent Black, 27 percent Hispanic, and 40— no, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. 25 percent Black. Our previous exam, 7001, which was held in 2016-2017, 25 percent Black, 27 percent Hispanic, and 44 percent white.
Those are— those are for the applicants?
Those are for the test takers.
The test takers. And then how many were hired? Were the— was the demographic breakdown similar?
The demographic breakdown is similar for those that were reachable. 18 percent Black–
Sorry, what do you mean by reachable?
Reachable, meaning they scored high enough on exam to be reached, to be processed.
Okay. So does that mean hired?
Not specifically, not necessarily. The hiring would be different.
Do you have the hiring numbers?
I don't have that on me. I don't have the numbers of those that were hired from the last exam. But we can very—
Can you follow up with that?
Absolutely, very easy to get that for you.

Okay, great. Thank you so much. And, also just want to express my gratitude for the entire department for everything that you do to keep New Yorkers safe, and we greatly appreciate it, and I would love to see more resources and more money and pay parity for EMS division. So thank you, and thank you, Chairs.

I just want to note that I was just given another list that actually the Fire Department gave our office in 2025 that were priority engine companies and EMS stations that needed– they were in terrible disrepair. And again, the engine companies that you gave, 325, 161, 54, 74, and 301, they're not even on your own priority list. You didn't take anyone off your own priority list. There's a reason for that?

Because those projects that were referred to were already funded. So they would have been higher priorities, but because we were able to allocate funding to them, they weren't on the unfunded list. And so as projects get funded, they will move off that unfunded priority list.
